hook.1: Asha: My first payslip came, and it says ₹18,000 at the top.
hook.2: Supervisor: That is your gross pay. Some amounts are deducted before the rest reaches you.
hook.3: Asha: Let's read the fictional payslip and find what I actually take home.

lesson.title: Read a fictional payslip
lesson.prompt: Tap the amount that is paid to Asha after deductions (take-home pay).

decision.title: Which amount reaches the account?
decision.prompt: This fictional payslip lists a retirement-savings contribution (assumed 12% of gross), tax deducted at source (assumed ₹400) and a canteen charge (assumed ₹500). Tap the take-home pay.

consequence.explanation: Gross pay is the total before deductions; net pay is what is left after them. Plan your budget around net pay. The rates and amounts here are assumptions for a fictional payslip.

transfer.prompt: Tap the amount this worker takes home after deductions.

dev.title: Dev's payslip lists net pay first and a bigger year-to-date figure. Find his take-home pay.

ila.title: Ila's payslip shows the employer's total cost too. Find her take-home pay.

claim.tds: For salary, the employer deducts tax at source (TDS) on the employee's behalf, using the employee's declarations to work out the amount.
claim.form16: Form 16 is the certificate of tax deducted at source on salary. The employer issues it to the employee at the end of the financial year.

gross_as_net.review: Your choice: you read an amount other than take-home pay as what you receive. Safer choice: use net pay, the amount after deductions, when planning spending. Concept: gross pay, deductions and net pay are different numbers; for salary, tax is deducted at source by the employer. Why it matters: budgeting from gross pay overstates what you can spend.
